records.name: Viral infection mechanisms: bounded scope
openObligations: The admitted observations concern MS2 bacteriophage. Other viral systems require separate evidence.

The three preparations are separate publications and separate contexts. Cell-free assembly dynamics, a reconstructed mature-particle structure and isolated-receptor association cannot be silently joined into one measured lifecycle.

No selected observation establishes proteolytic maturation, acquisition of infectious competence, complete genome delivery across a cellular boundary, productive intracellular replication, propagation or host-expression reprogramming.

A protein named maturation protein is a component label, not observation of the maturation process. A completed capsid or genome-containing structure is not a measured assembly trajectory; an optical assembly trajectory is not an infectious-competence assay.

No free-energy minimum, elementary rate constant, molecular critical-nucleus count or universal kinetic mechanism is inferred from a static structure. Reported finite optical changes remain conditional on the instrument/calibration and temporal resolution.
No physical-instance admission is made. Structural stoichiometry, specimen count or image-particle count is not an emergence minimum or carrier-equivalence rule.
No single admitted preparation measures entry, host exploitation, replication, assembly and propagation as a coordinated full infection program.
An isolated-receptor association, a static structure and separate cell-free assembly do not jointly measure the attachment-to-propagation sequence.
Transport, catalytic takeover, signaling and regulatory-environment exploitation are not measured by these selected high-level observations.
No host-expression, genome amplification or particle-production comparison supports controlled host reprogramming here.
The infection-program ontology is original classification, not a demonstrated multistage regime.
Intracellular takeover, processing, replication timing, coordinated production and transmission remain unsupported by the admitted structural/optical contexts.

records.name: Prepared yeast sugar-perturbation pH context
openObligations: The source observes pHluorin-expressing S. cerevisiae BY4741 and defined derivative strains in buffered medium after sugar changes. The source uses a standard-curve conversion; its earlier detailed calibration paper and raw points were not newly read.

The source Methods reports a roughly 30-second acquisition dead time followed by a 30-minute trace. Initial sub-dead-time events are not resolved, and a selected 10-minute genotype comparison is not itself a kinetic rate constant.

The pH differences establish a finite regulated response associated with the selected gene perturbations. They do not show all ionic species, a universal fixed setpoint, broad acid/base buffering, or pre-cellular homeostatic control.
PMA1 and other essential/severe-growth-defect genes were excluded from the deletion screen. Direct Pma1 flux and the complete pump-control mechanism are not established by these genotype contrasts.
The authors speculate about positive feedback through Gpa2. Neither a recovery trace nor a genetic endpoint establishes that specific closed feedback loop, gain or dynamical stability.

The study reports typical assay uncertainty and independent-experiment summaries. These are source statements, not an independently replayed calibration or uncertainty budget; no absolute pH values or numerical effect sizes are newly extracted.

The separate metabolite MS, purified Gpa2 unfolding and structural informatics are outside the admitted acquisition here. Total ATP abundance must not be treated as ATP production flux, free nucleotide potential or direct pump activity.

studies.finding: Yeast pH recovery depended on glucose availability. Under limiting glucose, selected sugar-sensing deletions yielded less acidification than wild type, whereas loss of Snf1 yielded more. Combined pathway perturbations and Gpa2 rescue comparisons support a regulated, preparation-specific intracellular-pH response.
limitations: The source observes pHluorin-expressing S. cerevisiae BY4741 and defined derivative strains in buffered medium after sugar changes. The source uses a standard-curve conversion; its earlier detailed calibration paper and raw points were not newly read.

The source Methods reports a roughly 30-second acquisition dead time followed by a 30-minute trace. Initial sub-dead-time events are not resolved, and a selected 10-minute genotype comparison is not itself a kinetic rate constant.

The pH differences establish a finite regulated response associated with the selected gene perturbations. They do not show all ionic species, a universal fixed setpoint, broad acid/base buffering, or pre-cellular homeostatic control.
PMA1 and other essential/severe-growth-defect genes were excluded from the deletion screen. Direct Pma1 flux and the complete pump-control mechanism are not established by these genotype contrasts.
The authors speculate about positive feedback through Gpa2. Neither a recovery trace nor a genetic endpoint establishes that specific closed feedback loop, gain or dynamical stability.

The study reports typical assay uncertainty and independent-experiment summaries. These are source statements, not an independently replayed calibration or uncertainty budget; no absolute pH values or numerical effect sizes are newly extracted.

The separate metabolite MS, purified Gpa2 unfolding and structural informatics are outside the admitted acquisition here. Total ATP abundance must not be treated as ATP production flux, free nucleotide potential or direct pump activity.
